ripgrep searches the contents of files by using rg <pattern> <path>, like rg Controller app/ to find all mentions of Controller in the directory app.
This tool is also used by Neovim when you type Space S G.
The full manual can be found via man rg.
Print only the paths with at least one match and suppress match contents.

Note that it is possible for this flag to have results inconsistent with the output of -c/--count. Notably, by default, ripgrep tries to avoid searching files with binary data. With this flag, ripgrep might stop searching before the binary data is observed. But with -c/--count, ripgrep has to search the entire contents to determine the match count, which means it might see binary data that causes it to skip searching that file. To avoid this inconsistency without disabling binary detection, use the --binary flag.
Option text matches rg --help / man rg (see rg/manpage).

Whenever a file path is printed, follow it with a ASCII/C0/NUL byte. This includes printing file paths before matches, and when printing a list of matching files such as with -c/--count, rg/-l aka rg/--files-with-matches and --files. This option is useful for use with xargs.
Option text matches rg --help / man rg (see rg/manpage).
When this flag is present, ripgrep will use the PCRE2 regex engine instead of its default regex engine.
This is generally useful when you want to use features such as look-around or backreferences.

Using this flag is the same as passing --engine=pcre2. Users may instead elect to use --engine=auto to ask ripgrep to automatically select the right regex engine based on the patterns given. This flag and the --engine flag override one another.

Note that PCRE2 is an optional ripgrep feature. If PCRE2 was not included in your build of ripgrep, then using this flag will result in ripgrep printing an error message and exiting. PCRE2 may also have worse user experience in some cases, since it has fewer introspection APIs than ripgrep's default regex engine. For example, if you use a \n in a PCRE2 regex without the -U/--multiline flag, then ripgrep will silently fail to match anything instead of reporting an error immediately (like it does with the default regex engine).
This flag can be disabled with --no-pcre2.

Using rg, how can I display + or - 8 lines of context around a match, plus line numbers?
Symmetric context (8 lines before and after each match): use -C 8 or --context=8, e.g. rg -n -C8 PATTERN path/. -C is shorthand for the same line count with -B and -A together.
Using rg, how can I display + or - 8 lines of context around a match, plus line numbers?

Asymmetric context (+8 after only / −8 before only): use -A 8 (--after-context=8) for lines after the match, or -B 8 (--before-context=8) for lines before. You can combine them independently, e.g. rg -n -B3 -A8 PATTERN (3 before, 8 after). Order matters when mixing with -C: later flags partially override earlier ones (see rg --help under -C).

The overall shape of the risks a tool, dependency, system, or decision carries: what can go wrong, how likely it is, and how much it would expose.
A profile is understood, not just measured — the goal is a mental model legible enough to reason about before committing.
Every choice to adopt a tool or design pattern imports its failure modes along with its benefits.
Comparing options is less about feature counts and more about which option's risk profile is easier to hold in your head and defend.
A small, well-understood set of risks is safer than a larger set that is individually milder but collectively opaque.
More entry points, dependencies, and configuration knobs widen the profile. My/Principle/Simplify/Minimize Surface Area.
Fewer, deeper choices concentrate risk where it can be scrutinized
Consolidating on fewer tools that are more secure yields a more understandable profile. My/Principle/Simplify/Fewer and Deeper.
Fewer, deeper choices concentrate risk where it can be scrutinized
Well-chosen standards and sensible defaults inherit the vetting of a broad community; bespoke variants carry undocumented risk. My/Principle/Simplify/Prefer Standards and Defaults.
A lower risk profile does not mean fewer features — it means the residual risk is bounded and explainable.
More security controls do not automatically improve the profile if they add complexity no one fully understands.

Every choice that could pay off could also go wrong, and the two arrive together: the options with the largest upside carry the widest spread of outcomes, and the options with the narrowest spread pay the least. Weighing risk against reward means deciding how much uncertainty to accept in exchange for how much expected gain. The answer turns on how much a loss would cost, whether it could be recovered from, and how many more times the same choice will come around.

The tension appears in investing, where it is stated as a premium demanded for bearing volatility; in engineering, where a faster or cheaper design carries more ways to fail; in choosing tools and dependencies, where capability comes with surface area; and in personal decisions about what to publish, share or keep private.
Size the bet by the worst case and the ambition by the best case. A loss that would end the game is never worth its expected value; a loss that is small and recoverable can be taken many times over.
Prefer choices whose risk is legible. Risk/Profile argues that a small, well-understood set of risks beats a larger set that is individually mild and collectively opaque.
Repeated choices favor the higher expected value. A one-shot choice favors the narrower spread.
Separate the risk that is paid for from the risk that is not. Exposure that could be avoided or spread out adds variance with no added reward.
Risk/Profile describes the shape of the risk a tool, dependency or decision carries.
My/Principle/Balance/Risk vs Reward/wrt Privacy - Make Things As Public As They Can Be applies the trade-off to what to share in public.
Reaching for reward means choosing the option with the largest expected gain.
Gains — the upside itself: return, capability, reach or learning that the cautious option leaves on the table.
Costs — the risk that comes attached, since the options with the most reward carry the widest spread, and the habit of counting the upside while discounting the downside.

Too far — chasing: taking on any exposure that promises a payoff, until the accumulated spread swamps the expected gain. Its mirror image is leaving reward on the table out of habit, taking only what is certain and small.
Accepting risk means choosing an option whose outcomes spread wide, including outcomes that lose.
Gains — access to payoffs that safe options never reach. The spread is what makes the large upside available at all, and bearing it is what the reward pays for.
Costs — the chance of loss, the attention it takes to hold the exposure in mind, and the compounding damage when a loss cannot be recovered from.
Too far — ruin: a single bad draw that ends the game, so no later reward is ever collected. A portfolio, a project or a reputation staked on one outcome.

The add command can either scaffold one Rulesync feature file or append one declarative source to rulesync.jsonc. See rulesync/Skill/Declarative Source for the source-fetching workflow this feeds.
A feature keyword creates a valid, editable starter file

Named features accept a name with or without the .md suffix. Skills use the directory layout .rulesync/skills/<name>/SKILL.md; other named features create <name>.md in their canonical directory. Names cannot contain path separators.

When the target file exists, interactive execution asks before replacing it; declining leaves it unchanged. JSON, silent, and non-interactive execution fail safely — pass --force to overwrite explicitly.

Feature keywords are reserved when no source-specific option is present. To add a source whose identifier is also a feature keyword, supply a source option that makes the intent explicit, e.g. rulesync add skill --transport npm.

For any other source identifier, add appends one source to rulesync.jsonc, preserving JSONC comments, and immediately runs the declarative source resolver: it installs selected rules into .rulesync/rules/.curated/, selected skills into .rulesync/skills/.curated/, and updates rulesync.lock or rulesync-npm.lock.json.

The selected configuration file must already exist — run rulesync init first, or pass --config <path>. Adding a source whose normalized identity is already present fails rather than silently duplicating lockfile entries; edit the existing entry instead.

Only the source being added is fetched; existing declarations are not re-fetched, and they must already be locked/installed (run rulesync install first if not). The operation is transactional: if the new source fails to install, Rulesync restores the manifest, source lockfiles, curated rules, and curated skills to their pre-command state.
When neither --skills nor --rules is given, all skills are installed for backward compatibility. Providing only --rules installs no skills.
